v.why: With edge 4 absent, removing edge 5 leaves only edge 0->3 feeding the output, cutting all deep conv paths (e.g. exp 24, a drop of about 16-19 points).
A strong direct conv on edge 0->3 makes the output less dependent on node 2, so dropping edge 5 hurts less (exp 41 even gained).
Replacing the conv on the final edge with a parameter-free skip removes key capacity (exps 57 and 70 dropped 4-12 points).
Swapping the conv on edge 2->3 for pooling removes learned capacity on the main output path (exps 72 and 84).
Upgrading a parameter-free direct input-to-output edge to a 3x3 conv adds large capacity (exps 18 and 64 gained 2-10 points).
Replacing pooling on edge 0->3 with a conv gave very large gains (exps 78 and 86), unlike replacing a skip (exps 75 and 85).
A skip in place of pooling on edge 0->3 helps (exps 23 and 40), whereas a skip in place of a conv hurts badly (exp 92).
Replacing pooling on edge 0->1 with a skip keeps node-1 information intact (exp 14 gained 10-15 points), while replacing a conv loses capacity (exps 48 and 62).
When edge 0 is none, node 1 carries no signal, so an edit on edge 1->3 has almost no effect and cannot deliver the usual gain.
When edge 5 is none, node 2 never reaches the output, so adding a conv on edge 0->2 is wasted (contrast exp 74, where edge 5 was a conv and the edit gained 4-10 points).

raw:
I based these on the 100 measured edits plus how the cell's wiring works. Three patterns come up repeatedly in the data:

- **Path to the output.** Edits matter most when they change whether a convolution sits on a path to node 3.
- **Dead edges.** If a node has no live input, or no live output, edits on edges touching it have no effect.
- **What gets replaced.** Swapping a pooling or skip edge for a convolution helps much more than swapping one convolution for another.

None of these were tested as interactions. They are hypotheses picked from patterns in single edits.
